name: Daria Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts with the laptop, not the cows. Stonebridge, the Van Dijks' dairy out by the old railway bridge, has two hundred and forty cows and three milking robots, plus wheat and grass for silage. The robots milk round the clock, so at six I check the overnight list: which cows didn't come in, which ones have a high cell count, which ones the robot flagged as lame. Then I go and find them. I came here a year ago after fifteen years on a hotel front desk, so the cows are new but the screens aren't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle. The robot says cow 418 is off, and I go and work out why. Sometimes it's her foot, sometimes she's just bullied at the feed fence. What wears me out is the hands-on stuff I'm still bad at. Hanna, the Van Dijks' daughter, can put a cow in the crush in two minutes. It takes me ten and I'm covered in muck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, we've already got the useful bits. The milking robots work, the chat tools help me plan, and that's probably as good as it gets for a while. I'd say it to Hanna, and maybe in the dairy group I'm in online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I like this stuff. I'd hoped the robot would get good enough to tell me why a cow's lame, not just that she is. But it also means I have time to get good at the hands-on side, which I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI every day to sort the robot reports and write up the vet visits. I'd ask the Van Dijks if I can do the hoof-trimming course in the spring. And I'd keep the money as it is: we've savings and Marek's and my little rental flat in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're restless. What would you want to change if nothing big happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to try things on my own. Marek and I have talked about a farm-stay, a couple of rooms for city families. I know hotels, I know booking systems. In a quiet world, that's my next step in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Marek see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek's a plumber, self-employed. He thinks robots will never fit a boiler in a cupboard under the stairs. He's probably right for a while. He's the calm one in our house.

S0.say: I'd say we already have the useful bits, the milking robots and chat tools for planning, and that may be as good as it gets for a while. I'd say it to Hanna and in my online dairy group.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I like this stuff and hoped the robot would one day tell me why a cow is lame. But it gives me time to get good at the hands-on side.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily to sort robot reports and write up vet visits, and asks to do the hoof-trimming course in spring. Leaves savings and the rental flat as they are, with a farm-stay idea for later.
S0.quote: I'd hoped the robot would get good enough to tell me why a cow's lame, not just that she is.
S0.fieldNote: Daria already works alongside milking robots and treats the farm as a puzzle read off screens. A plateau leaves her mildly disappointed and restless for her own project. Her hotel background shows in a farm-stay idea she's discussed with her partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for farms, mostly. Farms have been short of people for years. I'd tell the dairy group, learn the tools or get left behind, and I'd mean it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a good spot. I'm the person at Stonebridge who reads the robot data. If there are more machines, there's more data. The bit I'm less needed for is the muck, and I'm bad at that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask the Van Dijks to let me set up the new kit when it comes, cameras for lameness and feed pushers, because I already know their systems. I'd use AI more to analyse the herd. And I'd start the farm-stay early, as a side thing, maybe two rooms in the Van Dijks' old cottage if they'd rent it, because people will want real farms more if everything else is screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Like the week before a hotel reopening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people will want real farms more. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the hotel, the busier and more online people got, the more they paid for a fire and a walk. I think families will pay to let their kids see a calf born. I'd bet a bit of money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Stonebridge would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel, the relief milker. He's fifty-five, he does the old jobs, scraping, bedding. He doesn't want screens. I'd try to get him onto the farm-stay side, showing kids the calves. He's brilliant with children.

S1.say: I'd say it's mostly good news for farms, which have been short of people for years. I'd tell my dairy group, kindly, to learn the tools or get left behind.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm well placed, since I'm the one at Stonebridge who reads the robot data. The part of the job I'd lose is the muck, and I'm bad at that anyway.
S1.do: Asks to set up the farm's new lameness cameras and feed pushers and uses AI more to analyse the herd. Starts a small farm-stay side business early, hoping to rent two rooms in the Van Dijks' old cottage.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the week before a hotel reopening.
S1.quote: At the hotel, the busier and more online people got, the more they paid for a fire and a walk.
S1.fieldNote: She talks like someone running a small business, pragmatic and without blame. Steady change looks like more data for her to read and a market for a farm-stay. She's already thinking about moving an older colleague into a role that suits him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a mess, and the government and the big companies both need to keep things working while it settles. I'd say it without much heat. Shouting doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is the first to go in that picture. If AI can do anything, it can read the robot data better than me, and the robots can fix the lame cow too. We're fine on money, the rental flat brings in a bit and we've savings, but my plan for the next ten years disappears in two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the farm-stay straight away. I'd put maybe fifteen thousand of our savings into doing up the cottage, if the Van Dijks would do a long lease. I'd use every AI tool I can to run the bookings and marketing cheaply. Whatever's human about a farm is what I'd sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared. More like the night before a big opening when you're not sure anyone will come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put fifteen thousand in. Isn't that a risk if people have less money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If everyone's out of work, who books a farm holiday? I'd thought of that. But if prices fall because robots make everything cheap, maybe people still spend on the things they can't get from a machine. I'd take the bet, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zofia and Kuba?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zofia's thirteen, she'd want to help with the website. I'd let her. Kuba's ten, he'd ask if he can still feed the calves. I'd say yes, that's the whole point.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be a mess, and government and big companies both need to keep things running while it settles. I'd say it calmly, because shouting doesn't help.
S2.think: My job would be one of the first to go, because AI would read the robot data better than me. We're fine for money with the rental flat and savings, but my ten-year plan would disappear in two.
S2.do: Speeds up the farm-stay plan straight away, putting about fifteen thousand of savings into doing up the cottage on a long lease. Uses AI tools to run bookings and marketing cheaply.
S2.feel: Uneasy but not scared, like the night before an opening when you don't know who'll come.
S2.quote: If everyone's out of work, who books a farm holiday? I'd thought of that.
S2.fieldNote: She sees clearly that her screen-based role is exposed and responds by moving faster, not slower. She names the main risk in her own plan without being asked twice. Her money and her partner's trade work give her room to take a careful bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd say that to anyone, at the school gate, online, at the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd ride the robot wave for a bit and then step off. Maybe I'd go and work for the milking robot company itself, as the person who trains farms to use their kit. I'd be useful for three years at least, and I'd learn how they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the robot company as a field trainer in the first year, they're always hiring people who've used the machines on a real farm. I'd keep the farm-stay plan going slowly with Marek, maybe open in year three. I'd put a bit into the rental flat to keep it nice, because people will still need homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy. I'd quite enjoy it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would leaving Stonebridge be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I like the Van Dijks, and Hanna's been patient with me. But they'd understand. Their own plan is to sell to a bigger farm in a few years anyway, they've told me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about in that five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek. Plumbing feels safe now, but five years is enough for a robot to learn the cupboard under the stairs. I'd want him to pick up the heat pump side, the newer stuff, while there's time.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now, and I'd say it at the school gate, online and at the farm.
S3.think: With five years I'd ride the robot wave for a while and then step off, maybe working for the milking robot company itself. I'd be useful for at least three years and learn how they think.
S3.do: Applies in the first year to the milking robot company as a field trainer for farms. Keeps the farm-stay plan going slowly with Marek for an opening in year three, and spends a little on keeping the rental flat in good order.
S3.feel: Calm and busy, even enjoying it.
S3.quote: Plumbing feels safe now, but five years is enough for a robot to learn the cupboard under the stairs.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan in stages: a job with the robot maker, then the farm-stay. Her worry shifts to her partner's trade, which she'd push towards newer heat pump work. She's at ease leaving her employer, who plan to sell anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if you use it. Most people won't, they'll wait till year eight. I'd say that kindly too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fifty-three, the kids are grown, the house is nearly paid. I'd have done the robot company, then the farm-stay, and maybe the farm-stay is the thing I retire into. I'm not worried for me. I'd worry about people who wait till year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Stonebridge a couple more years, learn the cows properly, the hoof trimming, the calving. Then the robot company job. I'd plan the farm-stay for year five. I'd talk to Zofia about what she studies, because she'll finish school right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the cows properly. Why bother if robots will do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the farm-stay needs someone who really knows animals, not just screens. A family wants the woman who can tell them why the calf is wobbly. I want to be that woman, not just the one with the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do something where you're the one people trust. A vet, a teacher, a nurse. Use the AI, of course, but be the face. She rolls her eyes when I say that. She's thirteen.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if you use it, though most people will wait till year eight. I'd say that kindly as well.
S4.think: At fifty-three, with the kids grown and the house nearly paid, I'd have done the robot company and then the farm-stay, maybe retiring into it. I'm not worried for me, more for the people who wait.
S4.do: Stays at Stonebridge for a couple of years to learn hoof trimming and calving properly, then moves to the robot company. Plans the farm-stay for year five and talks with her daughter about what to study.
S4.quote: A family wants the woman who can tell them why the calf is wobbly. I want to be that woman, not just the one with the laptop.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she'd deliberately invest in hands-on skills, because her end goal is a farm-stay that sells real knowledge. She's relaxed about herself and worried about people who leave it late. Her advice to her daughter is to be the trusted face who uses AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for the money, for the plan. I'd lose ten years of steps in one go. What would help is simple rules for small businesses, so you can open a farm-stay or a shop without six months of forms. And some way to borrow cheaply to start something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the cows, maybe. People think robots are cold, but our cows love the milking robot. They come in when they want, no one shouting. If AGI is like that for people, it might not be all bad.

headlineQuote: People think robots are cold, but our cows love the milking robot. They come in when they want, no one shouting.
portrait: Daria Novak is 43 and a year into work at a dairy farm with three milking robots, after fifteen years on a hotel front desk. She uses AI every day to read the robots' reports and plan her work, and she's still slow at the hands-on jobs. Pragmatic and business-minded, she blames no one and plans in stages: run the farm's new kit, work for a robot maker, then open a farm-stay with her plumber husband. She stays calm in most scenarios and uneasy only when AGI arrives in two years, which would wipe out her plan in one go.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would wipe out her ten-year plan in one step.
whatWouldHelp: Simple rules that let small businesses like a farm-stay open without months of forms, and cheap loans to start something.
